idiom_name: copy into a temporary, then commit with a non-failing exchange (RAII or the collector releases the old state)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the type a copy operation that produces a complete independent value and a commit operation that cannot fail (a member-wise exchange, a single reference store, or an atomic publish). Perform every step that can fail -- allocation, deep copying, validation -- while the target is still untouched, then commit with the non-failing step, and let the temporary's owner (destructor, defer/finally block, or the garbage collector) release the previous state. The temporary is what keeps the old state alive until the new one exists, so the guarantee needs no rollback code and no error path inside the assignment; the price is a full copy per assignment and a commit that must genuinely not fail.
code_sketch:
assign(target, source):
    tmp = complete_copy_of(source)   # fallible: build the new state off to the side
    swap(target, tmp)                # infallible commit; tmp now owns the old state
    return target                    # release of the old state is automatic
pitfalls: Failing part way through the copy is acceptable only because the temporary is discarded; a commit step that can fail (allocating swap, validating store) breaks the guarantee entirely.
Sharing state between target and temporary instead of exchanging ownership turns the commit into aliasing: both objects own the same resource and release it twice.
The copy must be complete before the first observable change; any write to the target before the commit reintroduces the window the pattern removes.

The commit step itself must be genuinely non-throwing: if swap can allocate or a store can fail, the strong guarantee collapses to basic, and a throw from a noexcept-marked operation calls std::terminate.

Buffer reuse is impossible: even when the target's existing capacity would suffice, the idiom always allocates a new temporary and discards the old buffer -- a performance penalty for a safety guarantee that may not have been required.

Wrong move: implementing move assignment as T& operator=(T o) { swap(*this, o); return *this; } because it mirrors the copy form -> the target's old resources stay alive until the end of the full expression instead of being released or reused at the assignment, doubling peak memory and surprising callers about release timing (Meyers, 2014) -> instead write move assignment against an rvalue-reference parameter that frees or reuses the target's resources, and reserve the by-value-and-swap form for copy assignment where the strong guarantee is the point.

Wrong move: applying copy-and-swap to vector-like members whose capacity matters -> every assignment silently discards the target's reserved capacity and reallocates, measured from ~70% slower on average to almost 8x slower than capacity-aware assignment when the target could have reused its buffer (Hinnant, ACCU 2014) -> instead use assign()/in-place copy with the basic guarantee where capacity reuse or speed matters, and reserve() explicitly when you want different capacity behavior.

Wrong move: assuming assignment through the standard library gives you what copy-and-swap would -> std::vector's own copy assignment promises only the basic guarantee precisely to avoid the idiom's mandatory reallocation, so code that leans on it gets weaker safety than intended -> instead construct a replacement and swap it at the call sites that genuinely need the strong guarantee, rather than retrofitting the idiom everywhere.
